mainTopic: Guarantor's relatives as witnesses, retrying a condemned fugitive, courts in and outside ארץ ישראל, how rarely to execute, and the start of the laws of גלות
overview: The amud opens with a short story. Two witnesses were relatives of a ערב (guarantor), and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע shows רב פפא that the guarantor is a side in the loan, so his relatives cannot testify. Then a new משנה teaches that a condemned man who fled is not retried, and that a סנהדרין functions both in ארץ ישראל and outside it. The same משנה records how rarely the תנאים think a court should execute anyone. The גמרא resolves an apparent contradiction in the משנה: according to אביי and a ברייתא, a verdict from abroad is reopened in ארץ ישראל, but a verdict from ארץ ישראל stands everywhere. It finds a פסוק showing that courts apply everywhere, and explains that בשעריך requires a court in every city only in ארץ ישראל. It leaves one question as תיקו: what רבי אלעזר בן עזריה means by 'once in seventy years'. It then explains how רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא would avoid executions through very demanding questions to witnesses, while the other חכמים follow שמואל. Finally the chapter ends with a הדרן, and the next chapter's משנה begins listing which accidental killers go into גלות. Its contrasting cases continue on the next amud.

steps.title: The guarantor's relatives sign as witnesses
steps.stepSummary: אילעא and טוביה, relatives of the ערב, signed as witnesses, and רב פפא thought they were valid because they are not related to the borrower or the lender.
steps.simpleTranslation: אילעא and טוביה were relatives of the guarantor. רב פפא wanted to say: compared to the borrower and the lender, they are distant (not related).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case about witnesses who were related to the guarantor of a loan. רב פפא gives his first opinion that their testimony is fine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Relatives cannot testify about a case they are connected to. רב פפא's thinking is that the loan is really between the לוה and the מלוה, and these witnesses are not related to either of them. So in his view the guarantor's family does not matter.

keyTerms.meaning: The guarantor, who backs up a loan
He thought to say (a first opinion that will probably be rejected)

phrases.english: Ile'a and Tuviyya,
were relatives of the guarantor.
Rav Pappa thought to say:
With regard to the borrower and lender, they are distant.
phrases.notes: He means they are not related to the two main sides of the loan, so they should be valid witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion of disqualified witnesses with a practical case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: First opinion: relatives of the guarantor may testify, because they are unrelated to the borrower and the lender.

steps.title: The lender can collect from the guarantor
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע rejects רב פפא's opinion: if the borrower cannot pay, the lender collects from the guarantor, so the guarantor is part of the loan.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע said to רב פפא: If the borrower has nothing, doesn't the lender go after the guarantor?
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע pushes back on רב פפא with a question. The guarantor is also a side in the loan, so his relatives cannot be witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא saw the loan as involving only the borrower and the lender. רב הונא points out that the guarantor can end up paying, so he has a real stake in the document. That makes his relatives unfit to testify about it.

keyTerms.meaning: If he does not have (money to pay)
Isn't it so? (a question that expects 'yes')

steps.whatToRemember: A guarantor counts as a side in the loan, so his relatives are disqualified as witnesses on the loan document.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ לְרַב פָּפָּא:
phrases.english: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, said to Rav Pappa:
If the borrower does not have the money,
doesn't the lender go after the guarantor?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ לְרַב פָּפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב פפא's first opinion.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Fully rejects רב פפא's view that the guarantor's relatives are valid witnesses.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב פפא overlooked that the guarantor can be made to pay, so he is a real side in the loan.

steps.title: A condemned man who fled is not retried
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a person sentenced to death who ran away and came back before the same court is not retried. Two witnesses who testify that he was already sentenced are enough to execute him.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone whose death sentence was decided, who ran away and came before that same court, does not have his verdict reopened. Wherever two people stand and say, 'We testify that so-and-so was sentenced in such-and-such court, and so-and-so and so-and-so were his witnesses,' he is executed.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches that once a death sentence is final, running away does not earn the person a new trial.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first case is about the same court, so it simply carries out its own earlier verdict. The second line widens this: in any place, testimony that a court already sentenced him is enough, without a new trial. This difference between the two lines is what the גמרא will soon ask about.

keyTerms.meaning: His verdict was finished, meaning he was sentenced

phrases.english: MISHNA
One whose verdict was delivered, and he fled,
and he came before that same court,
they do not overturn his verdict.
Any place where two will stand and say:
"We testify about a man, so-and-so,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנִּגְמַר דִּינוֹ בְּבֵית דִּין שֶׁל פְּלוֹנִי,
phrases.english: that his verdict was delivered in the court of so-and-so,
and so-and-so and so-and-so were his witnesses",
that person shall be executed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New משנה, separate from the story about the guarantor.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A final death sentence is not reopened. Testimony that a court already sentenced the person is enough to execute him.

steps.title: A Sanhedrin functions in Israel and outside it
steps.stepSummary: The משנה teaches that a סנהדרין operates both in ארץ ישראל and in חוץ לארץ.
steps.simpleTranslation: A סנהדרין is in effect in the Land and outside the Land.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a short new rule about where a סנהדרין that judges capital cases can function.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, the משנה spoke about one court and one condemned man. Now it states a general rule: the authority of a סנהדרין is not limited to ארץ ישראל.

keyTerms.meaning: A court of judges able to rule on capital cases

phrases.english: A Sanhedrin is in effect in the Land and outside the Land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה with a new rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A סנהדרין operates both in ארץ ישראל and outside it.

steps.title: How often may a court execute?
steps.stepSummary: A סנהדרין that executes once in seven years is called destructive. רבי אלעזר בן עזריה says once in seventy years. רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא say they would never have executed anyone. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל warns that this would increase murderers.
steps.simpleTranslation: A סנהדרין that executes one person in seven years is called destructive. רבי אלעזר בן עזריה says: one in seventy years. רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא say: If we had been in the סנהדרין, no person would ever have been executed. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: They too would increase murderers in Israel.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings a debate among the תנאים about how rarely a court should carry out the death penalty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The opinions move from 'once in seven years is already too much', to 'once in seventy', to 'never'. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל pushes back: if courts never execute, the death penalty no longer scares anyone, and more people will commit murder.

keyTerms.meaning: Destructive, harmful (a court that is too quick to execute)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic source about balancing extreme care for human life with the need for law to protect society.
steps.whatToRemember: The תנאים want executions to be extremely rare. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל warns that never executing anyone would remove the fear of punishment.

phrases.english: A Sanhedrin that executes one in a seven-year period
phrases.notes: Here שבוע means a cycle of seven years, not a week.

phrases.english: is called destructive.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says:
One in seventy years.
Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say:
If we had been in the Sanhedrin,
no person would ever have been executed.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:

phrases.aramaic: אַף הֵן מַרְבִּין שׁוֹפְכֵי דָּמִים בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל.
phrases.english: They too would increase murderers in Israel.
phrases.notes: "They" means רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא, whose approach would remove the fear of punishment.

steps.triggerLanguage: סַנְהֶדְרִין הַהוֹרֶגֶת אֶחָד בְּשָׁבוּעַ נִקְרֵאת חוֹבְלָנִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's discussion of the סנהדרין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A court should execute only very rarely. The opinions range from once in seven years being too many, to never executing at all, which רבן שמעון בן גמליאל opposes.

steps.title: Inference: another court would retry him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads an inference from the משנה: only the same court does not reopen the case, which suggests a different court would.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: It is before that same court that they do not overturn. But before a different court, they do overturn.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts by drawing an inference from the משנה's first line. This step sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה specifically said 'that same court'. The גמרא reads this precisely and concludes that a different court would reopen the verdict and hold a new trial.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA

phrases.aramaic: לִפְנֵי אוֹתוֹ בֵּית דִּין הוּא דְּאֵין סוֹתְרִין,
phrases.english: It is before that same court that they do not overturn,

phrases.aramaic: הָא לִפְנֵי בֵּית דִּין אַחֵר – סוֹתְרִין.
phrases.english: but before a different court, they do overturn.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִפְנֵי אוֹתוֹ בֵּית דִּין הוּא דְּאֵין סוֹתְרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the גמרא's analysis of the משנה's first line.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Inference from the משנה: a different court would retry the condemned man.

steps.title: The later clause says he is executed anywhere
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the inference: the later clause of the משנה says that in any place, testimony of an earlier sentence is enough to execute him, with no new trial.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the later clause teaches: Any place where two stand and say, 'We testify about so-and-so that he was sentenced in such-and-such court, and so-and-so and so-and-so were his witnesses,' that person is executed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's later clause again to challenge the inference it just made. 'Any place' sounds like no court retries him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first line suggested that only the same court refuses to retry. The later clause says that anywhere, testimony of an earlier sentence leads to execution, which suggests that even a different court does not retry. The two lines of the משנה seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: The later clause (end part) of a משנה

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new משנה. The גמרא is repeating the later clause of the same משנה in order to use it against the inference from the first line.

phrases.english: But the later clause teaches:
Any place where two will stand and say:
"We testify about a man, so-and-so,
that his verdict was delivered in the court of so-and-so,
and so-and-so and so-and-so were his witnesses",
that person is executed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the inference made in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that a different court would retry the condemned man.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The later clause says 'any place', which means testimony about the earlier sentence leads to execution even before another court. That contradicts the inference from the first line.

steps.title: אביי: One clause is about Israel, the other is about abroad
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the two clauses of the משנה describe different directions of travel. Coming into ארץ ישראל means a retrial. Fleeing out of ארץ ישראל means no retrial.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: It is not difficult. Here it is about ארץ ישראל, and there it is about outside the Land.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the challenge from Step 7 by saying the two parts of the משנה are talking about two different cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first clause, which implies that a different court reopens the case, is about someone sentenced in חוץ לארץ who comes before a court in ארץ ישראל. The later clause, which says to just execute him, is about someone sentenced in ארץ ישראל who comes before a court in חוץ לארץ. So the two clauses do not clash.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. This introduces an answer that shows there is no real contradiction.

steps.confusionAlert: Each 'כאן' (here) tells you where the person ended up, meaning which court he now stands before. It does not tell you where he was first sentenced.

phrases.english: Abaye said: It is not difficult.
Here, it is in Eretz Yisrael,
phrases.notes: This is the first clause. He was sentenced abroad and now stands before a court in Israel, so they retry him.

phrases.english: there, it is outside the Land.
phrases.notes: This is the later clause. He was sentenced in Israel and now stands before a court abroad, so they do not retry him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in Step 7
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each clause is about a different direction of travel
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both clauses seemed to describe the same case, so they appeared to contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Coming into ארץ ישראל leads to a retrial. Leaving ארץ ישראל leads to no retrial.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports אביי's split between Israel and abroad
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בן דוסתאי, quoting רבי שמעון בן שטח, rules that someone who fled from ארץ ישראל abroad keeps his verdict. Someone who came from abroad into ארץ ישראל gets his verdict reopened, because of the merit of ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught: רבי יהודה בן דוסתאי says in the name of רבי שמעון בן שטח: If he fled from the Land to outside the Land, they do not overturn his verdict. If he fled from outside the Land to the Land, they overturn his verdict, because of the merit of ארץ ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says exactly what אביי just said, as support for his answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא states both directions explicitly. A verdict from ארץ ישראל stands even abroad, but a verdict from abroad is reopened in ארץ ישראל. The reason given is the merit of ארץ ישראל, which may help the court find a way to clear him.

keyTerms.meaning: They overturn his verdict and judge him again

steps.whatToRemember: A verdict from ארץ ישראל is final everywhere. A verdict from חוץ לארץ is reopened if the person comes to ארץ ישראל.

phrases.english: As it is taught in a baraita:
Rabbi Yehuda ben Dostai says
in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Shataḥ:
If he fled from the Land to outside the Land,
they do not overturn his verdict.
If he fled from outside the Land to the Land,
they overturn his verdict,
because of the merit of Eretz Yisrael.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source that supports אביי's answer
steps.raayaObject: אביי's split between ארץ ישראל and חוץ לארץ
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא of רבי יהודה בן דוסתאי in the name of רבי שמעון בן שטח

steps.title: Where do we learn that a סנהדרין works outside Israel?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves on to the next line of the משנה and asks for the source that a סנהדרין operates in חוץ לארץ as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: "A סנהדרין is in effect" etc. From where are these matters derived?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It quotes the משנה from Step 4 and asks for its source, setting up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said a סנהדרין operates both in ארץ ישראל and in חוץ לארץ. The גמרא wants to know which פסוק teaches this.

keyTerms.meaning: From where are these matters derived? This asks for the source of a law.

phrases.english: "A Sanhedrin is in effect" etc.
From where are these matters derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic, the next line of the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source that a סנהדרין operates in חוץ לארץ

steps.title: The source: "for your generations" applies everywhere
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns from the פסוק "for a statute of justice for your generations" that a סנהדרין operates both in ארץ ישראל and outside it.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the רבנן taught: "And these shall be for you as a statute of justice for your generations". We learn that a סנהדרין is in effect in the Land and outside the Land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a ברייתא that brings a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about judging murderers says it is a law "for your generations" and, at its end, "in all your dwelling places". This shows that the court system is not limited to ארץ ישראל.

keyTerms.meaning: A statute of justice, a permanent law of judgment

phrases.english: As the Rabbis taught:
"And these shall be for you
as a statute of justice for your generations",
phrases.notes: במדבר 35:29. The פסוק goes on: "in all your dwelling places."

phrases.english: we learn that a Sanhedrin is in effect
in the Land and outside the Land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 10
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק in במדבר 35:29 teaches that a סנהדרין applies everywhere.

steps.title: But the Torah says courts are "in your gates"
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks: if courts apply everywhere, why does the Torah say judges should be appointed "in your gates," which sounds like ארץ ישראל only?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what does the verse teach by saying "in your gates"?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא challenges its own conclusion with a different פסוק that seems to limit courts to ארץ ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Your gates" suggests the cities of the Jewish land. If courts are required abroad too, this word seems to have no purpose, so the ברייתא asks what it comes to teach.

keyTerms.meaning: What does the verse come to teach? This asks why a word is needed.
In your gates, meaning your cities

phrases.english: If so,
what does the verse teach by saying "in your gates"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion of Step 11 with another פסוק
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a סנהדרין applies outside ארץ ישראל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word בשעריך seems to limit courts to ארץ ישראל, so it would be pointless if courts apply everywhere.

steps.title: Every city in Israel, but only every district abroad
steps.stepSummary: "In your gates" teaches that in ארץ ישראל courts are set up in every district and every city. In חוץ לארץ they are set up in every district but not in every city.
steps.simpleTranslation: In your gates you set up courts in each and every district and in each and every city. Outside the Land you set them up in each and every district, but you do not set them up in each and every city.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers that "in your gates" is about how many courts are needed, not about whether courts exist at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both places must have courts. The word בשעריך adds an extra requirement only for ארץ ישראל: a court in every single city. Abroad, one court per district is enough.
steps.whatToRemember: A סנהדרין applies everywhere. In ארץ ישראל there must be a court in every city, while abroad a court in every district is enough.

phrases.english: In your gates you set up courts
in each and every district
and in each and every city,
and outside the Land you set up courts
in each and every district,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אַתָּה מוֹשִׁיב בְּכׇל עִיר וָעִיר.
phrases.english: but you do not set them up in each and every city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 12
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the פסוק: בשעריך refers to how many courts are needed, not to whether courts exist
steps.terutzHavaAmina: בשעריך seemed to limit courts to ארץ ישראל only.
steps.terutzMaskana: Courts are required in every city in ארץ ישראל, and only in every district in חוץ לארץ.

steps.title: What does 'once in seventy years' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רבי אלעזר בן עזריה means a סנהדרין that executes once in seventy years is destructive, or that once in seventy years is the normal rate.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said a סנהדרין that executes once in seven years is called destructive, and רבי אלעזר בן עזריה said once in seventy. The question: does he mean that even once in seventy years makes it destructive? Or does he mean that once in seventy years is normal, so only more than that is destructive?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה and asks how to understand רבי אלעזר בן עזריה's words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His words can be read two ways. Reading one: one execution in seventy years already earns the label 'destructive.' Reading two: one execution in seventy years is the acceptable normal pace, and only executing more often than that is destructive.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised before the חכמים (an open question they were unsure about)
Destructive, a court that kills too easily
The normal way of things, standard conduct

phrases.english: A Sanhedrin that executes, etc.
A question was raised before them:
Is one that executes once in seventy years called destructive,
or perhaps that is the normal way?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next line of the משנה after finishing the topic of courts in חוץ לארץ.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether 'once in seventy years' is the point at which a court counts as destructive, or the normal acceptable pace.

steps.title: The question is left unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The question stays open: תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא cannot settle the question and leaves it open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תיקו means no proof was found either way. Both readings of רבי אלעזר בן עזריה remain possible.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand: the question remains unresolved

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question from step 14 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: We do not know which reading of 'once in seventy years' is correct.

steps.title: How would רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא avoid executions?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical method רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא would have used so that no one was ever executed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא say: 'If we had been on the סנהדרין, no one would ever have been executed.' How would they have done that?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's next line and asks how this claim would actually work in court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Witnesses can give clear testimony that someone committed murder. So the גמרא wants to know what these two תנאים would have done to keep such a case from ending in a death sentence.

phrases.english: Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say:
If we had been, etc.
phrases.notes: The משנה continues: 'in the סנהדרין, no person would ever have been executed.'

phrases.english: How would they have acted?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical method for avoiding a death sentence in a murder case.

steps.title: They would ask: was the victim a טריפה?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר explain that they would ask the witnesses whether the victim was a טריפה or healthy, which no witness can know for sure.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר both say: they would ask the witnesses, 'Did you see whether he killed a טריפה, or whether he killed a healthy person?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 16 for murder cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who kills a טריפה is not executed. A witness cannot see inside the victim's body, so he cannot be sure the victim was healthy. Without that certainty, the testimony cannot lead to a death sentence.

keyTerms.meaning: A person with a fatal internal defect; killing him does not bring the death penalty
Whole, healthy, without such a defect

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר דְאָמְרִי תַּרְוַיְיהוּ:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar both say:
Did you see whether he killed a tereifa,
phrases.notes: These are the questions the judges would put to the witnesses.

phrases.english: or whether he killed a healthy person?

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר דְאָמְרִי תַּרְוַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 16 for murder cases.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Ask the witnesses whether the victim was a טריפה, which they cannot know.

steps.title: Even a healthy-looking body proves nothing
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי adds that even if the body was checked and found healthy, there may have been a hole exactly where the sword went in.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Even if you say the victim was found to be healthy, perhaps there was a hole in an organ right where the sword cut, and the wound now hides it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי strengthens the answer from step 17 by blocking an easy way around it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might suggest examining the body after death to show the victim was not a טריפה. רב אשי replies that the sword wound itself could hide an earlier fatal hole. So the doubt can never be fully removed.

keyTerms.meaning: Even if you say (granting a point for argument's sake)
A hole or puncture in an organ, which makes a person a טריפה

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Even if you say he was healthy,
perhaps there was a hole in the place of the sword.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds to step 17 so that checking the body cannot remove the doubt.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sword wound could hide an earlier fatal hole, so the victim's healthy status can never be proven.

steps.title: What about cases of forbidden relations?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how they would have avoided executions for someone accused of relations with an ערוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the case of someone who has relations with a forbidden relative, how would they have acted?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the same question from step 16 to a different capital crime.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The טריפה question only works for murder. Forbidden relations are also capital crimes, so a different method is needed there.

keyTerms.meaning: One who has relations with a forbidden relative (a capital crime)

phrases.aramaic: בְּבוֹעֵל אֶת הָעֶרְוָה הֵיכִי הֲווֹ עָבְדִי?
phrases.english: With one who has relations with a forbidden relative, how would they have acted?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּבוֹעֵל אֶת הָעֶרְוָה הֵיכִי הֲווֹ עָבְדִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the question of step 16 to a different crime.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The method for avoiding a death sentence in forbidden-relations cases.

steps.title: They would demand very exact testimony
steps.stepSummary: אביי and רבא say they would ask whether the witnesses saw the act itself in full detail, which witnesses almost never see.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי and רבא both say: they would ask the witnesses, 'Did you see it like a brush going into a tube?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 19.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By demanding that the witnesses actually saw the act itself, they set a standard that witnesses almost never meet. Without it, the testimony would be incomplete and no execution could follow.

keyTerms.meaning: A small brush or stick used to apply eye paint

phrases.english: Abaye and Rava both say:
Did you see it like a brush in a tube?
phrases.notes: This is a modest way of asking whether they saw the actual act itself up close.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Require the witnesses to have seen the act itself in detail.

steps.title: How do the other חכמים judge such cases?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the חכמים, who do not follow רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא, would convict in forbidden-relations cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן, how do they judge?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about the other side: the חכמים who do not take this approach.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Detailed testimony is almost impossible to get. So the גמרא asks what level of testimony the other חכמים think is enough to convict.

keyTerms.meaning: The חכמים, here meaning those who do not follow this approach

phrases.english: And the Rabbis, how do they judge?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא's approach to the other חכמים.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What testimony the other חכמים consider enough to convict.

steps.title: Seeing them act like adulterers is enough
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים follow שמואל: witnesses can testify once they see the couple acting like adulterers, without seeing the act itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: They follow שמואל, because שמואל said: with adulterers, testimony is valid once the witnesses see them behaving the way adulterers behave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 21 by quoting שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים do not require graphic detail. If the witnesses saw the couple in the position and behavior of adulterers, that is enough to convict. This is the opposite of the strict standard in step 20.

keyTerms.meaning: Once they appear to be acting as adulterers

steps.whatToRemember: רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא would block executions by asking questions witnesses cannot answer: was the victim a טריפה, and did they see the act itself. The other חכמים follow שמואל, so seeing the couple behave like adulterers is enough testimony.

phrases.english: In accordance with Shmuel, as Shmuel said:
With adulterers, once they are seen as adulterers.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Witnesses only need to see the couple behaving as adulterers.

steps.title: הדרן: closing the chapter כיצד העדים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא formally closes פרק כיצד העדים.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter 'How are the witnesses'.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the traditional closing line marking the end of the פרק about עדים זוממין. No new law is taught here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הדרן signals that the discussion of lying witnesses is finished. The next line starts a completely new topic, the laws of גלות.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you: the formula for finishing a chapter
Name of the first פרק of מכות, about lying witnesses

steps.whatToRemember: The topic of עדים זוממין is now closed; a new subject, accidental killers and exile, begins.

phrases.english: We will return to you
chapter 'How are the witnesses'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the entire chapter that ended with the discussion of how the חכמים convict in forbidden-relations cases.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The chapter on lying witnesses is complete.

steps.title: Accidental killings that lead to exile
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה states that an accidental killer goes into exile and gives three examples: rolling a roller, lowering a barrel, and coming down a ladder.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are the people who go into exile: someone who kills a person by accident. If he was rolling a roller and it fell on someone and killed him, or he was lowering a barrel and it fell on someone and killed him, or he was coming down a ladder and fell on someone and killed him, this person goes into exile.
steps.whatsHappening: The new משנה opens the laws of גלות. It says that someone who kills by accident is exiled, and gives three cases where this applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Not every accident leads to exile; the details of how it happened matter. In all three cases here, the object or person was moving downward when the death happened. The משנה will soon contrast these with cases that do not lead to exile.

keyTerms.meaning: Goes into exile to an עיר מקלט (city of refuge)
A heavy roller used to smooth a plastered roof

steps.whyThisMatters: This משנה sets up the whole chapter: exile is for a specific kind of accidental killing, and the direction of the motion turns out to be a key detail.

phrases.english: MISHNA: These are the ones who go into exile:
one who kills a person by accident.
If he was rolling a roller
phrases.notes: A roller is a heavy stone cylinder people rolled over a plastered roof to smooth it.

phrases.english: and it fell on him and killed him,
phrases.notes: 'Him' here means the victim, not the person doing the work.

phrases.english: or he was lowering a barrel
and it fell on him and killed him,
or he was going down a ladder
and he fell on him and killed him,
phrases.notes: Here the man himself falls, so read it as 'he killed him.' The word in square brackets is the corrected wording, and it leaves out the word in round brackets.

phrases.english: this person goes into exile.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a brand-new chapter and topic after the Hadran.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An accidental killer is exiled in cases like rolling a roller, lowering a barrel, or coming down a ladder and falling on someone.

steps.title: Contrasting cases: pulling a roller or lifting a barrel
steps.stepSummary: The משנה begins listing contrasting cases, pulling a roller and lifting a barrel when the rope snaps, whose ruling comes next.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he was pulling the roller and it fell on someone and killed him, or he was lifting up a barrel and the rope snapped and it fell on someone and killed him...
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה sets up a contrast with the earlier cases. It describes the situations here, and the ruling for them comes right after this section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These cases look almost the same as the earlier ones, but the motion is different: pulling toward himself and lifting up, instead of rolling and lowering down. The word אבל (but) tells us these cases will get a different ruling than 'he goes into exile'.
steps.confusionAlert: The sentence is not finished yet. Do not decide the ruling from this section alone; the משנה gives it in the very next words.

phrases.english: But if he was pulling the roller
and it fell on him and killed him,
or he was lifting up a barrel
and the rope snapped
and it fell on him and killed him

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: מימרא (continuation of the same משנה statement)
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets up the opposite side of the contrast to the cases that lead to exile.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה presents pulling a roller and lifting a barrel as contrasting cases; their ruling follows in the next part of the משנה.
